question.text: The distance $d$, in meters, a falling body travels after being released from rest varies directly with the square of the time $t,$ measured in seconds, since the body was released. If the body covers $12$ meters in $2$ seconds, then what is the constant of variation?
question.explanation:
The distance $d$ is directly proportional to the square of the time $t$, so we have \[ d = kt^2, \]

where $k$ is the constant of variation.

We are told that $d=12\,\textrm{m}$ when $t=2\,\textrm s.$ We can use this information to solve for $k,$ as follows:

\begin{align*} 12 &= k \cdot 2^2 \\[5pt] 12 &= k \cdot 4 \\[5pt] \dfrac{12}{4} &= k \\[5pt] 3 &= k \end{align*}

Therefore, the constant of variation is $k=3.$

example.title: Modeling Direct Variations With Second Powers

question.text: The surface $S,$ in square centimeters, of a cylinder whose height equals the radius of its base varies directly with the square of its radius $r,$ measured in centimeters. If the surface is $16\pi\,\text{cm}^2$ when the radius is $2\,\text{cm},$ then what is the constant of variation?
question.explanation:
The surface $S$ is directly proportional to the radius $r,$ so we have \[ S = kr^2, \]

where $k$ is the constant of variation.

We are told that $S=16\pi\,\text{cm}^2$ when $r=2\,\text{cm}.$ We can use this information to solve for $k,$ as follows:

\begin{align*} 16\pi &= k \cdot 2^2 \\[5pt] 16\pi &= k \cdot 4 \\[5pt] \dfrac{16\pi}{4} &= k \\[5pt] 4\pi &= k \end{align*}

Therefore, the constant of variation is $k=4\pi.$

example.title: Modeling Direct Variations With Second Powers

question.text: The electrostatic force $F,$ in newtons ($\mathrm N$), exerted between two identical charged particles kept at a fixed distance apart, varies directly with the square of the charge $q$ of each particle, measured in coulombs $(\mathrm C).$ If the electrostatic force is $8\,976\,\mathrm N$ when the charges are $2\,\mathrm{C},$ then express $F$ in terms of $q.$
question.explanation:
The electrostatic force $F$ is directly proportional to the square of the charge $q,$ so we have \[ F = kq^2, \] where $k$ is the constant of variation.

We are told that $F=8\,976\,\textrm{N}$ when $q=2\,\textrm{C}.$ We can use this information to solve for $k,$ as follows: \begin{align*} 8\,976 &= k \cdot 2^2 \\[5pt] 8\,976 &= k \cdot 4 \\[5pt] \dfrac{8\,976}{4} &= k \\[5pt] 2\,244 &= k \end{align*}

Therefore, our direct variation equation is \[ F = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{2\,244q^2}. \]
